title: Breach Breakdown: How One Server Move Left DigiCert Customer Data Exposed
description:
DigiCert, a certificate authority that issues the digital certificates browsers use to trust websites, says an unauthorized account read archived business customer data between June 27 and July 2, 2026. The root cause was a February 2025 server move that made an internal system reachable from the internet. Here is the timeline, the three root causes, what was and was not exposed, and four lessons for any organisation.

Timeline (from DigiCert's own incident report)
- February 4, 2025: an internal business system is moved and becomes reachable from the internet.
- June 18, 2026: staff notice non-DigiCert accounts, but wrongly conclude they had no data access.
- June 27 to July 2, 2026: an unauthorized account reads a small proportion of archived data; a fix on July 2 ends the access.
- October 19, 2026: DigiCert confirms the data access and that the incident is reportable. Preliminary report filed October 20.

Root causes (per DigiCert)
1. The move was treated as an infrastructure change, not a security change, so it skipped a security review.
2. A self-registration feature let outsiders create accounts without multi-factor authentication.
3. Accounts with no assigned application could still read archived data, and there was no alerting on new account creation.

What was exposed
Mostly names, business email addresses, phone numbers and business addresses. For a small minority of records, identity documents such as passports, driving licences or utility bills. DigiCert has not said how many customers were affected. It reported the incident to law enforcement and told The Record it has no evidence the information was misused.

What was not affected (per DigiCert)
No certificate operations, customer login credentials or issued certificates. Customers do not need to replace active certificates.

Four lessons (Securidge analysis)
1. Treat every network change as a security change.
2. Check permissions in the app, not just the network.
3. Alert on new accounts and unusual traffic.
4. If you are a customer, watch for phishing that uses your business details.

Sources
- DigiCert incident report on Mozilla Bugzilla, bug 2084460 (preliminary report October 20, 2026; full report posted as comment 2): https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2084460
